youtube.title: Python OOP Project: Build a Library System | Python Programming EP 72
youtube.description: In this episode you will design a small program with two classes, let one object hold other objects and avoid a shared mutable default, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Two classes, one idea · 0:59 Book and Library · 1:53 A library holds books · 2:25 Second program · 3:28 Recap · 3:58 Bug of the Day · 4:46 Challenge · 5:06 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Time to put classes together. We build a tiny library with books you can borrow and return.

scenes.onScreen: "Two classes, one idea": three numbered lines (1. Book: title, author, whether it is borrowed; 2. Library: a list of books and the actions on them; 3. Library methods use Book methods) and an analogy card: a real library: books are things, and the library is the thing that looks after them
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A good design starts by listing the things. Here we have books, and a library. A Book knows its title, its author, and whether it is out. A Library holds a list of books. It has actions, such as add a book, borrow, and list what is available. The library does not need to know how a book tracks borrowing. It just asks the book. Think of a real library. The books are things. The library looks after them.

scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The Book class. [HL 2] Init stores a title and an author. [HL 5] And that the book is not borrowed. [HL 7] Repr gives a readable line. [HL 10] The Library class. [HL 12] Its own list of books, fresh for every library. [HL 14] Add puts a book on the list. [HL 17] Borrow looks through the books. [HL 19] Right title, and not already out. [HL 20] Mark it as borrowed. [HL 21] And hand it over. [HL 22] Otherwise, nothing, which is None. [HL 24] Available builds a list of books still on the shelf. [HL 27] A library. [HL 28] Add two books. [HL 30] Borrow Python 101. We get the book. [HL 31] Borrow again. It is out, so None. [HL 32] And only Crab Tales is available.

scenes.onScreen: The name lib tied to a Library object; its list holds two Book objects
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The name lib is tied to a library object. Inside it sits a list of books. Each book is its own object, with a title, an author, and a borrowed flag. Objects can hold other objects. That is how bigger programs are built, from small objects that each do one job.

scenes.onScreen: members.py: a Member class that uses the library
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A small Book class. [HL 3] A title. [HL 4] And a borrowed flag. [HL 6] A Member class. [HL 8] Each member has a name. [HL 9] And a list of loans, new for each member. [HL 11] Borrow checks the book. [HL 12] Already out, so [HL 13] False. [HL 14] Otherwise mark it borrowed. [HL 15] Remember the title in the loans. [HL 16] And return True. [HL 18] One book. [HL 19] Two members. [HL 21] Asha borrows. True. [HL 22] Ravi tries the same book, and gets False. [HL 23] Only Asha has a loan.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as members dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, members dot py. Python 101 by Rao, then None, then a list with Crab Tales by Xecxec. Then True, False, and the two loan lists.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: Design by listing the things: Book and Library. Two: A Library object holds a list of Book objects. Three: Each class does one job. Four: Create lists inside init, not in a default argument. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: a mutable default shared by every library
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We add a book to the north library, and it appears in the south library too. The default list in the init brackets is built only once, and every library without its own list shares it. No error appears. Use None as the default, and create a fresh list inside init.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the library project get a good grade? It was well catalogued.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw

bug.why: A default value is built once, when the function is defined. A list as a default is therefore shared by every call. Use None, and build a fresh list inside.

pun: "Why did the library project get a good grade? It was well catalogued."
challenge: Add a give_back(title) method to the Library that marks a borrowed book as available again. Test it.
challengeAnswer: def give_back(self, title): for book in self.books: if book.title == title: book.borrowed = False.

shorts.title: Design first
shorts.hook: "Start a program by listing the things."
shorts.script: Start a program by listing the things. In a library, we have books, and the library itself. A book knows its title and whether it is out. A library holds the books and offers actions. List the things, then write one class for each. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Design by listing things.

shorts.title: Objects hold objects
shorts.hook: "A library object holds a list of book objects."
shorts.script: A library object holds a list of book objects. Objects can hold other objects, and that is how bigger programs are built. Each class does one small job. The library asks the book, is this one borrowed, and the book answers for itself. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Objects hold objects.

shorts.title: Borrow method
shorts.hook: "The borrow method loops over the books."
shorts.script: The borrow method loops over the books. If the title matches, and the book is not already out, it marks the book as borrowed, and returns it. If nothing matches, it returns None. The second borrow of the same book gives None. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Borrow and check.

shorts.title: Shared default
shorts.script: A tricky bug. You write init with books equals empty list in the brackets. Add a book to the north library, and the south library has it too. A default value is built once, and shared. Use None, and build a new list inside. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Never default to a list.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the library project get a good grade?"
shorts.script: Why did the library project get a good grade? It was well catalogued. Your challenge. Add a method called give back to the Library. It takes a title, and marks the borrowed book as available again. Test it by borrowing and returning. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 72.
